APPAREL DECORATION PRICING · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

What does a decorated shirt actually cost you?

A job-costing calculator for custom apparel shops — screen printing, embroidery, or DTF. Put in your screens or digitising, your press or stitch time, your blank cost and your spoilage allowance, and get the real cost per piece, the break-even price, the margin at what you quoted, and the same job costed at every quantity tier from a dozen to two gross. The quantity break is the whole point: a dozen is not a gross with a smaller number on it.

Everything runs in this browser. Your blank costs, wages and press speeds are never uploaded — see the privacy note in the footer.

What to look at

What this does and doesn't do

This is arithmetic on numbers you supply: it totals what one job costs you and compares that to what the job earns. It does not know your blank supplier's price, your press's real throughput, your local wage rules, or what a customer in your town will pay — every one of those is an input you read off your own invoices, payroll and equipment. Treat the output as the cost floor underneath your own pricing decision, not a recommended price, and not a market rate.

Pricing a custom-made physical object where a one-off setup and machine time dominate a short run is not only an apparel problem. If you also quote printed parts, the 3D print price calculator does the same job for print time, filament or resin, failure rate and post-processing. Already running your shop through Printavo or a similar platform? See how this calculator differs — it costs a job before that number ever reaches a quoting system. Pricing jobs off a spreadsheet instead? See what a flat per-piece rate leaves out — setup spread over the wrong quantity, blanks bought without a spoilage margin, and embroidery machine time divided by heads when hooping should not be.

Common questions

How much should I charge for screen printing?

There is no single right number, because the cost side moves far more than the price side: the same design is a different job at 12 pieces than at 288, and a shop paying $3.10 for a blank has a different floor than one paying $6.40. Work out your own cost per piece first — screens, art, press time, ink, blanks with a spoilage allowance, and a share of overhead — then set the price above it by the margin you need. This calculator does that arithmetic on your own numbers; what your market will bear is a separate question it cannot answer.

Why does a 12-shirt order cost so much more per shirt than a 144-shirt order?

Because setup is per job, not per shirt. Burning, registering and reclaiming a screen costs the same whether you print a dozen or a gross, and a three-colour front plus a one-colour back is four screens either way. Spread over 12 pieces that setup can be several dollars a shirt; over 144 it rounds to cents. Quoting both off the same price list is the most common way a small run loses money, which is why the break table on this page costs the same job at every standard quantity tier.

Should I charge screen setup and digitising as a separate line?

Either works, and the calculator shows the consequence of each. Billing setup separately keeps the per-piece price honest and comparable, and it matters most on repeats: a second run of the same design owes no new digitising and no new art, so a shop that buried those in the per-piece price has to explain why the repeat is cheaper. Absorbing setup instead is fine as long as you know it is in there — enter what you actually bill as a setup fee and the break-even figure adjusts to only the setup the per-piece price still has to carry.

How do I price embroidery — per 1,000 stitches or per piece?

Per 1,000 stitches is the industry's shorthand for the machine time, and it is a reasonable proxy because run time really is proportional to stitch count. It hides two things this calculator makes visible. A multi-head machine sews several pieces in one cycle, so the machine minutes per piece are the cycle divided by the number of heads — while hooping is per piece per placement and is not divided by anything, which is usually what actually caps a shop's daily output. And digitising is a one-off for the design rather than a per-piece cost, so on a short run it is a far bigger share of the job than a stitch-count rate suggests.

Does anything I type here get uploaded?

No. Every calculation runs in this browser, and nothing you enter is sent anywhere — there are no accounts, no cookies, and no analytics vendor. If you use the save button, your numbers are written to this browser's own local storage on this device only, and the forget button deletes them. Anonymous feature counts (estimate, example_loaded, inputs_saved) are stored the same local way and can be switched off.

Also quoting printed parts? The 3D print price calculator prices a print from machine time, material, failure rate and post-processing — the same setup-plus-machine-time shape as a decoration job. The CNC machining quote calculator is the same shape again for a machined part, and adds the two things a decorated garment never has: material bought in whole bars or sheets with a yield, and an outside-process lot minimum. Running an embroidery machine? The embroidery shop quote calculator goes deeper on that one process: clock time across heads, a quantity-break table, and whether a flat per-1000-stitches rule loses money on small runs. Screen printing? The screen print job quote calculator prices a run from screens, press time and spoilage, with a price-break ladder and the break-even order size. Pricing banners, signs or vinyl? The sign shop job pricing calculator prices wide-format jobs from material with waste, print time, design and install.

Quoting a flat price per shirt regardless of the job? See what that flat rate hides — on this calculator's own defaults, the same $14-a-shirt price is a thin profit on a front-only run and a real loss the moment a back placement is added.

should-i-charge-extra-for-a-second-print.text:
← Screen printing and embroidery price calculator

Should I charge extra for printing on the back too?

It sounds like a small ask: “Can you throw the logo on the back too? It’s basically the same design.” It is not the same setup. A second print location is a second full set of screens to burn, register and reclaim — and quoting it at the front-only per-piece price gives that setup away without anyone deciding to.

Open the free screen printing and embroidery price calculator

A second placement doubles the screen count, not the design count

On this calculator’s suggested rates — a 3-color design, $18 to burn and register each screen — a front-only job uses 3 screens ($54). Adding an identical 3-color placement on the back is not "one more screen," it is another full set: 6 screens ($108). Including shared art time, total job setup rises from $65.80 to $119.80 — a jump the per-design intuition misses entirely, because the design itself did not change, only how many placements carry it.

What keeping the front-only price actually costs

On a 24-piece run quoted at $14 a piece either way, adding the back placement without repricing looks harmless — the job still turns a profit — but the numbers move a lot more than "a little extra ink":

LocationsBreak-even / pieceProfit at $14/pieceMargin
Front only$9.72$102.8130.6%
Front + back$12.41$38.2011.4%

Same price, same 24 shirts — but adding the back placement without repricing hands back $64.61 of what was supposed to be profit, and margin falls from a healthy 30.6% to 11.4%, well under a typical 40% target. The shop does not lose money on this job; it just does not know it gave away nearly two-thirds of the intended profit.

The gap shrinks per piece, but grows in real dollars

Because the extra screens are a one-off cost, spreading them over more pieces shrinks the per-piece hit — but the extra ink and the second press pass are a real cost on every single piece, and that part does not shrink. Net effect: the dollar amount actually at stake on a whole job grows with volume, even as the per-piece gap falls.

QuantityAdded cost / pieceAdded cost, whole job
24$2.69$64.61
72$1.19$85.84
144$0.82$117.68
288$0.63$181.36

A shop that eyeballs the per-piece gap as "basically nothing" at high volume is reading the wrong column: the whole-job number is the one that shows up in the bank account, and it keeps climbing the bigger the order gets.

This is not the same shape as a flat add-on

A second print location is a mix, not a single flat number: part of its cost (the extra screens) is fixed per job and shrinks per piece as the order grows, and part of it (ink and press-pass time) is a true per-piece cost that never shrinks. Pricing it as either "add a flat fee" or "add a flat percentage" misses one half of that shape — a percentage undercharges a small run's setup share, and a flat fee undercharges the per-piece run cost on a large one.

How to use the comparison

Open the screen printing and embroidery price calculator, set your own colors, screen cost, press speed and wage, and change “Print locations” from 1 to 2 to see the setup and break-even move on your own numbers — your rates will not match the defaults above, so the dollar figures will shift even though the shape of the gap (bigger per-piece at low volume, bigger in total at high volume) stays the same. This applies to embroidery and DTF too: switch method to see the same locations toggle move digitizing cost or film area instead of screens.

Common questions

Should I charge extra for printing on the back of a shirt too?

Yes. A second print location is not one more design on the same setup — it is its own set of screens. On a 3-color job, adding a 3-color back placement takes screen count from 3 to 6, which on this calculator's suggested rates raises total job setup from $65.80 to $119.80 for a 24-piece run. Quoting the second location at the same per-piece price as the first gives that setup away.

Does a second placement cost twice as much per piece?

No, and that is what makes it easy to under-price. The added cost per piece shrinks as the order grows — $2.69 a piece at 24 pieces, $0.63 a piece at 288 — because the extra screens are a one-off setup spread over more pieces. But the total dollars at stake actually grow with volume, from $64.61 at 24 pieces to $181.36 at 288, because the added ink and press-pass time is a real per-piece cost that scales with the order even as the setup share shrinks.

What happens if I quote the second location at the front-only price?

On the 24-piece worked example, quoting $14 a piece for a two-location job that actually costs $12.41 a piece to break even still turns a profit, but a much thinner one: $38.20 instead of the $102.81 the same price yields on a front-only job, and 11.4% margin instead of 30.6% — well under a typical 40% target. The shop is not losing money, but it is unknowingly giving up almost two-thirds of the profit that price was supposed to deliver.

vs-a-flat-price-per-shirt.html.text:
← Screen printing and embroidery price calculator

This calculator vs. a flat $14-a-shirt price

Names no specific product or company. This compares a free calculator against the generic pricing habit apparel decorators are shopped against every day: one flat "per shirt" price — commonly a "$14 a shirt" quote — charged the same regardless of decoration method, colour count, or how many placements the job actually needs.

First — the flat per-shirt price is right, and you should have one

A quote sheet or a walk-in customer needs a number before anyone has counted screens. "$14 a shirt" is a perfectly fine headline rate, and no calculator replaces having one. What follows is not an argument that the flat rate is wrong. It is what that same rate stops showing you the moment a job is real and you know its quantity, its decoration method, and how many placements it needs.

The worked example

Both columns below are this calculator's own shipped default shop rates — a $20/hr wage loaded 18% to $23.60/hr, $18 to burn and register each screen, $4.20 blanks with a 4% spoilage allowance, $5,200 of monthly overhead spread across 2,600 monthly pieces — on the same 12-shirt, 3-colour screen-print order, quoted at the same $14-a-shirt price either way. The only thing that changes between the two columns is whether the design is printed on the front only or on the front and the back.

QuestionFront only — 12 shirts, 1 placement, 3 coloursFront + back — the same 12 shirts, 2 placements, 3 colours each
What the flat $14/shirt price charges $168.00 — 12 × $14 $168.00 — 12 × $14, unchanged
Screens needed 3 — one per colour, one placement 6 — one per colour, at every placement
Setup cost (screens + art time) $65.80 $119.80
Blanks (13 purchased at 4% spoilage) $54.60 $54.60 — unchanged, same 12 shirts
Run labour and ink $7.20 $12.50 — a second press pass, twice the ink
Overhead share $24.00 $24.00 — unchanged
Total cost before any profit $151.60 $210.90
What the flat $14/shirt price actually nets $16.40 profit — a thin 9.8% margin −$42.90 — a real loss, not a thin margin
This calculator's break-even price per piece $12.63 $17.57
This calculator's price at a 40% target margin $21.06 $29.29 — $8.24 more, for the same $14/shirt headline

The two places the flat rate goes quiet

1. Setup is per placement, not per design

A flat per-shirt rate answers "what do I charge per shirt," not "how many screens this job needs." Both live inside the same $14 either way. The calculator splits them out — 3 screens on the front-only job, 6 screens the moment a back placement is added — so a second placement is a visible line item instead of one flat rate that happened to work out on the last job.

2. The same advertised rate does not scale with the job

This is the one that costs real money. The flat rate charges $14 a shirt whether the order is a single front placement or the same order printed front and back, but the cost behind it is not the same — on this calculator's own defaults, the flat rate still nets a thin profit on the front-only job and a real loss the moment a second placement is added, with nothing on the quote sheet to say so. A shop quoting "$14 a shirt" on every job can price the front-only orders fine and lose money on every one that turns out to need the back printed too.

When the flat per-shirt price is still the better tool

For a quote sheet, it plainly is. A walk-in customer or a phone quote cannot fill out a live calculator, and most people asking "how much for a shirt" want one number, not a form. The sensible arrangement is both: quote the flat rate to close the sale, then run this calculator once you know the quantity, the decoration method, and the placement count, to check whether that job's version of "the $14-a-shirt order" still covers cost — and, on a job with more placements than the one the flat rate was set against, whether it needs its own price instead.

Every figure on this page is this calculator's own worked example, computed from its own shipped default shop rates ($20/hr wage, 18% payroll load, $18 screens, $4.20 blanks, 4% spoilage, $5,200 monthly overhead over 2,600 monthly pieces), not a claim about any real shop's business or an industry benchmark. Your rates, wages, and overhead will produce different numbers — the point is which numbers to produce, not what they should come out to.

Common questions

Is a flat price per shirt wrong?

No, and it should not go away. A quote sheet or a walk-in customer needs one number, and "$14 a shirt" is a fine headline rate. The point of this page is not that the flat rate is wrong — it is that the same per-shirt number is charged whether the job is a single 3-colour front placement or that same front plus a 3-colour back, and only a real cost breakdown separates the two.

Does the flat $14-a-shirt price even cover a small front-only order?

On this calculator's own shipped defaults, yes, with room to spare on paper but not much on target margin. A 12-piece, one-placement, 3-colour job costs $151.60 in total before any profit. At $14 a shirt that is $168.00 in revenue — a $16.40 profit, a 9.8% margin, well under the 40% target margin this calculator ships with by default.

What happens to that same $14 price once a back placement is added?

It goes from a thin profit to a real loss. The identical 12-piece order printed front and back needs six screens instead of three, so total cost rises to $210.90 on this calculator's own defaults — and the same $14-a-shirt price still only brings in $168.00. That is a $42.90 loss, a -25.5% margin, on an order that looked exactly as biddable as the front-only one from the quote sheet.

Does the calculator replace the flat per-shirt price?

No, and it is not trying to. The flat rate is what you quote to close the sale. This calculator is what you run once you know the quantity, the decoration method, and the number of placements, to check whether that job's version of "the $14-a-shirt order" still covers cost — and, on a job with more placements than the one the flat rate was set against, whether it needs its own price instead.

vs-a-spreadsheet.html.text:
← Screen printing & embroidery price calculator

Screen printing & embroidery price calculator vs. a spreadsheet

A spreadsheet multiplies a per-piece rate by a quantity fine. It does not, on its own, spread a job's screens or digitising across the right quantity, round blanks up to cover spoilage, or divide embroidery machine time by heads while leaving hooping undivided.

Cost a real job →

Plenty of shops already track jobs in a spreadsheet: one column for the design, one for a per-piece rate, a formula that multiplies by quantity. That arithmetic is trivial and a spreadsheet does it fine once the rate is known. What it does not do on its own is derive the rate itself — setup spread over the quantity actually being quoted (screens per colour per placement, or digitising for an embroidery design), blanks bought with a spoilage allowance rather than exactly the order quantity, and, for embroidery, machine minutes divided by the number of heads while hooping stays undivided. Each needs its own formula, rebuilt correctly for every quantity, with nothing checking that a small run isn't still being quoted off a big run's rate.

What each tool answers.
QuestionWhere to answer it
What's a known per-piece rate times a quantity? Either one — a spreadsheet multiplies fine.
What does this job cost per piece once screens or digitising, blanks with spoilage, and machine time are all spread correctly across this quantity? This calculator — it derives the rate from your screens, digitising, press or stitch time, blanks and spoilage, recomputed for the quantity you type.
Why does the same design cost more per shirt at 12 pieces than at 288? This calculator's quantity-break table, which spreads the same one-off setup across every standard tier at once.
Are embroidery machine minutes and hooping minutes being divided by the head count correctly? This calculator — it divides only the machine cycle by heads and leaves hooping, done once per piece by hand, undivided.
Is the break-even price and the margin at a price already on the table, and are blanks covering spoilage? This calculator — both are computed automatically, with blanks rounded up to cover the spoilage percentage entered.
Keep a settled price list or a season-long job record? A spreadsheet or price list — this page answers one job at a time and remembers nothing once you leave.

This calculator derives the cost per piece, the break-even price, and the margin at a price you're already considering directly from the decoration method, quantity, setup, run time, blanks and spoilage figures you type — recomputed every time, with no formula to keep in sync across jobs or quantities.

It needs no account and nothing installed: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and every number you enter stays on this device — nothing is uploaded anywhere.

Common questions

Isn't a decorated shirt's cost just a rate per piece?

That multiplication is trivial and a spreadsheet does it fine once the rate is known. What it does not do on its own is derive the rate itself from a job's setup -- screens burned per colour per placement, or digitising for an embroidery design -- spread over the quantity actually being quoted. A single per-piece cell has no built-in notion that the same design costs far more per shirt at 12 pieces than at 288, so a shop using one blended rate for every order quietly loses money on the small ones and overcharges the large ones.

Why does a 12-piece order cost so much more per piece than a 144-piece order?

Because setup is per job, not per piece. Burning, registering and reclaiming a screen -- or digitising an embroidery design -- costs the same whether the order is 12 pieces or 288. Spread that flat cost over 12 pieces and it can be several dollars each; spread it over 288 and it rounds to cents. A spreadsheet holds this correctly only if someone builds a formula that divides setup by quantity and keeps it in sync every time either number changes -- this calculator recomputes it from the job's own setup and the quantity typed in, at six standard tiers at once.

What does a spreadsheet miss about blanks and spoilage?

Blanks are bought in whole garments, and a spoilage allowance is bought the same way. A spreadsheet cell that multiplies blank cost by the order quantity assumes zero misprints, so one ruined shirt on a 24-piece run means re-ordering a single blank and setting the job up again -- a cost far larger than the shirt itself. This calculator rounds the blanks purchased up to cover whatever spoilage percentage is entered, rather than assuming a perfect run.

Why does embroidery need heads and hooping tracked separately?

A multi-head embroidery machine sews several pieces in one cycle, so the machine minutes a single piece actually costs are the cycle time divided by the number of heads -- but hooping is done by hand, once per piece per placement, and is not divided by anything. A spreadsheet formula that divides the whole run time by heads, hooping included, understates labor; one that never divides overstates machine cost. This calculator applies the division only to the part of the cycle it belongs to.

Does this replace a shop's own price list or quoting spreadsheet?

No. A price list or quoting spreadsheet that a shop keeps for its standard jobs and repeat customers is still the right place to record settled prices. This page answers one question at a time -- what does this specific job's cost per piece, break-even price, and margin at the quoted price actually come to, given this job's method, quantity, setup, and blanks -- and nothing it computes is saved anywhere once you leave the page.

vs-printavo.html.text:
← Screen printing & embroidery price calculator

This calculator vs. Printavo

Printavo is a well-known paid shop-management platform for decorated-apparel businesses, built to run a shop's day-to-day quote-to-invoice workflow — online quote requests, invoicing and payment collection, production scheduling, and customer approvals, sold as an ongoing subscription and described on printavo.com. It is the kind of tool a shop reaches for once it needs to manage many jobs, customers, and a production calendar at once.

That is a different job from the one this page does. This calculator has no customer records, no invoicing, and no production schedule. It exists for the narrower task that comes before any of that: working out what one job actually costs per piece — from screens or digitising, press or stitch time, blanks with a spoilage allowance, and a share of overhead — and what it costs at every standard quantity tier, with nothing to sign up for.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I need to take online quote requests, send invoices, collect payment, and schedule production across many jobs. Printavo or a comparable shop-management platform — day-to-day workflow is not something this calculator attempts.
What does this specific job actually cost me per piece, given its screens or digitising, run time, blanks, and quantity? This calculator — free, instant, private, no account.
Why does a 12-piece order cost more per piece than a 288-piece order of the same design? This calculator's quantity-break table, which spreads the same one-off setup across each tier.
I already know my price matrix. I need to send a quote, invoice it, and track it through production. Printavo or a comparable platform — quoting, invoicing, and scheduling are not this calculator's job.
Do I need to create an account or sign up to use the tool? This calculator: no. Printavo is used through a paid subscription account.

Most shops get different value from each: Printavo (or a comparable platform) for running quotes, invoices, and production scheduling as an ongoing subscription, and a private calculator like this one for an instant, no-login check of what a job should cost before that number ever reaches a quoting system. This calculator's own output is a cost check, not a record of your shop's customers, quotes, or invoices.

It needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or a shop-management platform like Printavo?

They answer different questions. Printavo is a paid subscription platform built to run a decorator's day-to-day workflow -- online quote requests, invoicing, payment collection, production scheduling, and approvals -- once a shop already knows what to charge, described on Printavo's own site. This calculator does none of that. It is a free, browser-only page for the narrower job that comes before any of it: working out what a specific screen print, embroidery, or DTF job actually costs per piece from your own screens or digitising, press or stitch time, blanks, spoilage, and overhead, with no account and nothing uploaded. A shop that needs online quote requests, invoice collection, and a production calendar is looking for the wrong tool here; a shop setting or checking a price before it goes into a quoting system is in the right place.

Does Printavo tell me what to charge for a job?

Printavo quotes and invoices at whatever price a shop enters into its price matrix; it manages sending, tracking, and collecting on that price, not deriving it from screens, press time, stitch count, or blanks. This calculator does the opposite: it takes your decoration method, quantity, setup, run cost, blanks with a spoilage allowance, and overhead, and works out the cost per piece, the break-even price, and the margin at what you quoted -- the arithmetic a shop does before a price exists to put in a quoting system, not the quoting itself.

Is this page affiliated with Printavo?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Printavo or its parent company, Inktavo. Printavo is named here only to describe what this calculator is and is not.
